DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

The paper is clearly organised, and its core arithmetic (£810 a week, £42,120 a year, competitor midpoints) is correct. However, it has one outright factual error that reverses a recommendation, a material omission in the profit projection, and several claims (in both the paper and your summary) that the data does not support. As written, it should not go to the owners.

## Critical issues

### 1. The mushroom risotto has the *highest* margin, not the weakest
Table 1 shows this: the risotto margin is (£14.00 − £2.80) / £14.00 = **80%**, the best on the menu. Fish and chips is 69%, the burger 72%, the curry 75%, the steak 60% and specials 64%.

- Its cash profit per plate is £11.20, which is more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90).
- It is not uniquely the lowest seller. It ties with specials at 90 plates a week.
- The proposed replacement is "a seasonal vegetarian special." On current evidence, specials run at **64%** margin, so the swap would likely *lower* margin.
- The paper doesn't say whether the risotto is the only vegetarian main. If it is, removing it may also cost whole group bookings.

Proposal 5.2 rests entirely on a misreading of the table. It should be withdrawn or completely rethought. The summary's claim that this is "clear-cut" and "an easy improvement" is the opposite of what the data shows.

### 2. The profit projection ignores the beef cost rise in Section 4
Section 4 says beef rises 12% from 1 April, the same day the new prices start. Section 5.3 leaves this out:

| Dish | Current cost | +12% | Extra cost/plate | Plates/week | Extra cost/week |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | £4.70 | £0.50 | 260 | ~£131 |
| Steak | £10.40 | £11.65 | £1.25 | 120 | ~£150 |

- That is about **£281 a week** of added cost.
- The net gain falls from £810 to about **£530 a week (~£27,500 a year)**, roughly a third less than claimed.
- Much of the burger and steak increase is simply passing on the beef rise, not new profit.

### 3. The "about 71%" main-course margin depends on that omission
I reconstructed the margin from Table 1, assuming specials average about £15:

- **Current:** about 69.4%.
- **With the increases and no cost change:** about 70.8%. This is where "71%" comes from.
- **Including the beef rise:** about **69.2%**, slightly *below* today's figure.
- **Swapping risotto (80%) for a ~64% special** would reduce it further.

The claimed margin improvement largely disappears once Section 4 is taken into account.

### 4. VAT is not addressed
UK menu prices include 20% VAT. A £1.00 menu increase is only about £0.83 of net revenue, so the uplift could be overstated by about a sixth. The table margins may also be calculated on VAT-inclusive prices, which would overstate every margin. The paper should say whether its figures are gross or net of VAT.

## Factual inconsistencies

- **Trading days.** Section 2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five** days. The recommendation says "six trading days a week."
- **"We remain the value option."** Section 3 says our prices are currently the *lowest in the group*. After the increases, all three dishes would be above the cheapest competitor:
  - Fish and chips: £17.50 vs £16.95
  - Burger: £16.00 vs £15.50
  - Steak: £28.00 vs £27.00

  "Below the midpoint" is true. "The value option in the area" no longer is. The owners should be told the restaurant is giving up its lowest-price position.
- **Overall vs main-course margin.** The 70% target and the drop to 67% refer to *all courses*. The paper only addresses mains and gives no figures showing how a mains change restores the overall target.

## Weak or unsupported reasoning

- **"Volumes will hold" is asserted, not evidenced.** There is no sensitivity analysis. It would help to show break-even volume losses. For example, at the net gain of about £530 a week, losing even about 5% of covers across these dishes would erase a large share of it.
- **Repeat guests are not the same as price-insensitive guests.** Regulars are the guests most likely to *notice* increases. Combined with the decision not to draw attention to them (Section 6), this creates a trust risk the paper doesn't weigh.
- **The September 2024 precedent is thin.** "No visible effect on bookings" is anecdotal. Bookings are not plates sold, and the size of that increase isn't stated.
- **"Weekday lunch is a small share" is unsupported.** Friday and Saturday dinner are "just under half" of mains. That leaves over half across the other services, so lunch could be significant. A figure is needed.
- **The monitoring plan is confounded by seasonality.** Comparing April–May volumes with a January–February baseline mixes the price effect with normal spring and summer changes. Use the same weeks last year as the comparison. Also set action thresholds in advance, such as "if plates fall more than X%, we review."
- **"Two months of till data for every main course."** January and February are a seasonally unrepresentative period. Specials are lumped together, with no price or cost data.
- **Fish volatility.** Fish and chips carries the largest volume increase, yet fish costs are described as "volatile." There is no allowance for that risk.
- **Annualising.** Multiplying by 52 assumes no closures or holidays. This is minor, but worth noting.

## Recommended changes before submission

1. Withdraw or rework 5.2. The risotto is the highest-margin main, so present the real case for any change, if one exists.
2. Recalculate 5.3 net of the beef cost rise and on an ex-VAT basis. The realistic figure is likely about £22,000–£27,000 a year, not £42,000.
3. Recompute the main-course margin including the new costs, and show the link to the overall 70% target.
4. Fix the five- versus six-day error.
5. Replace "remain the value option" with an accurate statement of the new competitive position.
6. Add a volume sensitivity and break-even table, plus lunch versus dinner split data.
7. Use a year-on-year baseline and defined action triggers for monitoring.
8. Reconsider the "don't draw attention" approach, given the reliance on regular guests.

**Bottom line:** the fish and chips and burger and steak increases may well be justified, especially to pass through the beef rise. But the paper overstates the benefit by roughly a third or more and recommends removing its best-margin dish on the basis of a misread table. It is not yet "well evidenced" or demonstrably "low-risk."
